newsitem.title: USA: US says weak yen benefitting Japanese car makers.
newsitem.headline: US says weak yen benefitting Japanese car makers.

text.p: A U.S. report on car trade with Japan released Friday said the weakening yen was benefitting Japanese car makers at the expense of U.S. firms.
"Japan's international competitiveness and profitability benefitted from the decline in the yen in 1996," the report said.
The report by the U.S. Commerce Department and U.S. Trade Representative's Office to President Clinton noted that the yen depreciated over the course of 1996 and into 1997.
"With respect to international trade, there have been some signs that exchange rates are beginning to affect bilateral automotive trade," the report said.

It said that despite earlier gains after the 1995 car trade agreement was signed, sales in Japan by the Big Three U.S. automakers -- Chrysler Corp, Ford Motor Co. and General Motors corp -- began to level off during late 1996 and declined in the first three months of 1997.

"In contrast, sales of European-made vehicles (including those produced by the Big Three) to Japan began to grow faster, in part because the yen did not depreciate as much against these currencies," the report said.

U.S. auto makers have been complaining for months that the weakening yen against the dollar was hurting their sales to Japan and giving Japanese car makers a competitive edge in U.S. markets. A weak yen makes Japanese cars less expensive in the United States and U.S.-made car more expensive in Japan.

The Big Three auto executives met earlier this week with Vice President Al Gore to discuss the trade situation as well as other issues of concern to the auto industry, industry officials said. The executives are also trying to arrange a personal meeting with President Clinton to address their concerns about the yen.
The report said that imports of Japanese vehicles into the U.S. market began to increase in late 1996 and that in early 1997, Japanese car makers were starting grap a bigger share of the U.S. market.
President Clinton and Japanese Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto are scheduled to meet next Friday in Washington. U.S. officials have said trade concerns will be on the discussion agenda.
